questions.question: Describe how diamonds were discovered and explain why the dry diggings of 1870 to 1871 were more significant than the first finds.
questions.expected_answer: In 1867 Erasmus Jacobs found the Eureka, a diamond of about 21 carats, near Hopetown by the Orange River; in 1869 the Star of South Africa, about 83 carats, was bought from a Griqua shepherd for 500 sheep, 10 oxen and a horse, proving the area's wealth. Diggers worked the river gravels of the Vaal. In 1870 and 1871 diamonds were found in dry ground at Dutoitspan, Bultfontein and Vooruitzicht, and at Colesberg Kopje, the New Rush, in July 1871. These dry diggings lay in kimberlite pipes that went deep underground, so the deeper miners went the more diamonds they found, turning a rush into a long-term industry that drew tens of thousands of people.

questions.question: Name the four claimants to the diamond fields and explain how Britain came to annex Griqualand West.
questions.expected_answer: The Orange Free State, which had farms and officials there; the South African Republic, the Transvaal, which claimed land along the Vaal and granted a digging monopoly; Nicolaas Waterboer of the Griqua, advised by David Arnot; and Tswana chiefs of the Tlhaping and Barolong. The Keate Award of October 1871, by Natal's Lieutenant-Governor Robert Keate, ruled on the Transvaal's border in favour of Waterboer and the Tswana. Waterboer then asked for British protection, and High Commissioner Barkly proclaimed the diamond fields, including dry diggings claimed by the Free State, British territory as Griqualand West in October 1871.

questions.question: Explain Britain's motives for annexation and its consequences for the Orange Free State and the Griqua.
questions.expected_answer: Motives: to control the immense diamond wealth and revenue; to stop the Boer republics gaining an independent income and strength; to keep the road to the north open; to control labour, trade and guns. Consequences: the Free State protested strongly and in 1876 accepted 90 000 pounds in compensation; distrust between Britain and the republics grew. Griqualand West became a Crown colony in 1873, Kimberley was named, and it joined the Cape in 1880. The Griqua, in whose name annexation occurred, lost much of their land through land court decisions and purchases by speculators, became impoverished and rebelled unsuccessfully in 1878.
